articles.title: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
articles.summary: USC scientists have discovered a way to create a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells that can attack cancer and strengthen the body's natural defenses. By growing and modifying immature immune cells rather than mature ones, researchers developed a system that can continuously produce tumor-fighting cells inside the body.
articles.content:
Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses.

The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell, could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body. In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells established themselves in bone marrow, produced new immune cells, and slowed the progression of both blood cancers and solid tumors.

The USC Stem Cell-led team focused on a type of immature immune cell called granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs). These cells normally develop into macrophages and other immune cells that protect the body from infections and participate in immune responses. The researchers found that GMPs could be grown extensively in the laboratory while retaining their ability to develop into functioning immune cells. They could also be genetically modified to recognize specific cancer markers and strengthen broader immune responses.

"The study establishes a scalable and engineerable GMP platform for cellular immunotherapy and introduces concepts that we believe could have broad implications for both cancer immunotherapy and stem cell biology," said the paper's corresponding author Qi-Long Ying, MD, PhD, professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC.

Scientists Discover a Surprising Ability in Immune Cell Precursors

Beyond its potential applications in cancer treatment, the discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of how blood and immune cells develop.

Stem cells are known for their ability to self-renew, meaning they can repeatedly divide while maintaining their original properties. In the blood-forming system, this ability has traditionally been associated primarily with hematopoietic stem cells, which can produce all the major types of blood and immune cells.

Progenitor cells, by contrast, are further along in development and are already committed to producing a more limited range of cells. They are generally thought to have less capacity for long-term self-renewal.

The USC researchers demonstrated that GMPs can retain this ability under carefully controlled laboratory conditions. Rather than quickly maturing into other cell types, the progenitors continued multiplying while preserving their identity and their capacity to generate functional immune cells.

"The prevailing view has been that long-term self-renewal in the blood system is primarily a property of the hematopoietic stem cells that can generate any type of blood or immune cell," said Ying. "We found that, under the right conditions, GMPs can also self-renew, dividing extensively while keeping their identity and ability to produce functional immune cells. That gives us a scalable starting point for engineering cell therapies for cancer, infectious disease and potentially many other conditions."

This finding could be especially important for developing treatments that require large, reliable supplies of genetically engineered immune cells.

Why Macrophages Could Be Powerful Weapons Against Cancer

Macrophages are among the immune system's most versatile defenders. Their name comes from Greek words meaning "big eaters," reflecting their ability to surround and engulf bacteria, damaged cells, and other unwanted material.

They also help coordinate immune responses by sending signals that influence the behavior of other immune cells. Some macrophages can enter tumors and attack cancer cells, making them attractive candidates for cancer immunotherapy.

One particularly promising application involves solid tumors, which include cancers that form masses in organs and tissues. Existing therapies based on engineered T cells have achieved their greatest successes against certain blood cancers, but treating solid tumors has proven more difficult.

Macrophages offer a potentially different approach because they naturally migrate into tissues and can penetrate tumors. However, turning them into practical treatments presents several challenges.

Once macrophages have fully matured, they are difficult to multiply in large quantities outside the body. They are also challenging to modify genetically and can be damaged during freezing and storage, complicating the production and distribution of cell therapies.

Another problem occurs after administration. Mature macrophages often collect in organs such as the lungs and liver instead of spreading widely throughout the body. Their relatively rapid disappearance can also limit how long a treatment remains effective.

To work around these limitations, the scientists decided to begin at an earlier stage of immune cell development.

Creating a Renewable Supply of Cancer-Fighting Immune Cells

Rather than trying to manufacture large numbers of mature macrophages, first author Shi Yue, MD, of Ying's laboratory and his colleagues concentrated on GMPs, the progenitor cells that can produce macrophages.

The researchers developed a precisely defined mixture of chemicals that allowed GMPs to survive and multiply for extended periods in the laboratory. The mixture prevented the cells from prematurely developing into mature immune cells, preserving a renewable population of progenitors.

Even after extensive laboratory expansion, the GMPs maintained the molecular characteristics that defined them. Importantly, they also retained the ability to develop into functional macrophages and other related immune cells when needed.

This approach could make it possible to manufacture large numbers of engineered immune cells from a starting population that can be continually expanded, instead of repeatedly collecting and preparing mature cells.

To confirm that the method could be reproduced, collaborators in the laboratory of Ravi Majeti, MD, PhD, at Stanford University independently demonstrated that GMPs could be maintained for extended periods and genetically engineered. Their results provided additional support for the reliability of the technique and its potential use in future cell therapies.

Majeti, Director of the Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine at Stanford University, noted: "This method for the expansion and engineering of GMPs opens the door to numerous translational applications, much like T cell expansion and engineering. We have already demonstrated engineering of these cells to drive multiple potent functions, and there is a lot more to be explored."

Engineering Immune Cells to Recognize and Attack Tumors

The team next investigated whether these expandable progenitor cells could be programmed to fight cancer.

They genetically engineered GMPs to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This engineered receptor allows immune cells to identify a particular molecular marker on the surface of cancer cells, helping direct their activity toward tumors.

CAR technology is already an important part of cancer immunotherapy, particularly in treatments that modify a patient's T cells to recognize and attack cancer. The USC researchers explored whether a similar strategy could be applied to GMPs, allowing them to generate engineered macrophages and other immune cells.

The scientists also equipped some of the progenitor cells with an additional immune-activating signal. This modification was designed to recruit and stimulate nearby immune cells, including T cells, which can help mount a stronger attack against cancer.

The added signal offered another potentially important advantage. It remained effective even when the immune characteristics of donor cells did not match those of the recipient.

That finding raises the possibility of developing off-the-shelf treatments using cells manufactured in advance from donors. Unlike personalized cell therapies, which must be prepared separately using each patient's own cells, such products could potentially be produced in larger batches and made available to multiple patients.

Engineered Cells Slow Cancer Progression in Mice

After successfully expanding and engineering GMPs from both mice and humans, the researchers investigated their therapeutic potential in mouse experiments.

When administered to mice, the progenitor cells established themselves in the bone marrow and other locations responsible for blood cell production. These environments provided places where the GMPs could generate additional engineered macrophages and related immune cells.

This was an important difference from treatments using mature macrophages. Instead of relying solely on immune cells that may disappear relatively quickly, the progenitors could provide a continuing source of replacement cells from within the body.

The strategy may therefore help overcome the rapid clearance that has limited macrophage therapies, including approaches evaluated in recent clinical trials.

The researchers tested the engineered cells in mice with blood cancers and solid tumors. GMPs carrying CAR receptors slowed disease progression in both types of cancer.

The effects were even stronger when the progenitors carried both CAR receptors and the additional signal designed to activate other immune cells. This combination improved the treatment's ability to stimulate a broader antitumor response.

Although these findings are encouraging, the cancer-treatment results remain preclinical. Further research will be needed to establish whether engineered GMPs can be used safely and effectively in people, particularly if they are intended to persist and produce immune cells over extended periods.

Potential Applications Beyond Cancer Treatment

The scientists also explored whether their approach could help treat conditions involving defective immune defenses.

In a separate mouse experiment, they studied chronic granulomatous disease, an inherited disorder that interferes with the ability of certain immune cells to kill harmful microbes. People with this condition are particularly vulnerable to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections because their immune cells cannot eliminate some pathogens effectively.

When the researchers administered GMPs to mice with the disorder, the cells restored the animals' ability to fight bacterial infection.

This result suggests that renewable, genetically engineered immune cell progenitors might eventually have applications beyond cancer, including treatments for inherited immune deficiencies and potentially infectious diseases.

The broader lesson, according to the researchers, is that the developmental stage of an immune cell may be just as important as the genetic modifications used to turn it into a treatment.

By engineering cells before they fully mature, scientists may be able to create therapies that are easier to manufacture, more adaptable, and capable of maintaining a continuing supply of specialized immune defenders.

"Our study suggests that the future of immunotherapy may depend not only on designing better CAR receptors, but also on choosing the right developmental stage of the cell," said Ying.

About the Research

The study, published in Cell, is titled "Expansion and CAR engineering of granulocyte-monocyte progenitors for cellular immunotherapy."

Along with Ying, Yue, and Majeti, the research team included Zheng Guo, Crystal Pan, Xueyuan A. Jing, Tai Nguyen, Jiaqi Tang, Yanpui Chan, Humberto Contreras-Trujillo, Du Jiang, Xue Yan, Hang Xiang, Xugeng Liu, Xiao Wang, Ziyuan Wang, Natalie Shu, Daniel B. McKim, Rong Lu, and Chao Zhang of USC; Litao Tao and Celia Bloom of Creighton University; Asiri Ediriwickrema and Sebastian Koschade of Stanford University School of Medicine; and Yingxiao Shi of Harvard Medical School and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

Financial support came from the Chen Yong Foundation of the Zhongmei Group, a sponsored research project from Myelogene Inc., the L.K. Whittier Foundation, the Eli and Edythe Broad Innovation Award, the Ming Hsieh Institute for Research on Engineering Medicine for Cancer Award, the USC SBIR/STTR Planning Award, the Xia Research Fund, and the Wu & Jiang Research Fund.

Majeti also reported support from the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research. Guo received funding through the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine Predoctoral Training Fellowship.

articles.personality_title: USC scientists develop renewable cancer-fighting immune cells
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been working to improve cancer treatments by using the body's own immune cells to attack tumors. However, making enough immune cells that stay active in the body has been a big challenge.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of Southern California (USC) found a way to grow and modify immature immune cells called granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs). These cells can multiply many times in the lab and then develop into cancer-fighting cells inside the body. They also engineered these cells to recognize and attack tumors in mice, slowing the growth of blood cancers and solid tumors.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it creates a steady supply of immune cells that can keep fighting cancer over time, unlike current treatments that rely on mature cells which do not last long. It also opens the door to making off-the-shelf therapies that could be given to many patients without needing to prepare cells from each person individually.

**What's next step** – The researchers plan to continue testing their method to ensure it is safe and effective in humans. They also want to explore if these engineered cells can treat other diseases, such as inherited immune problems or infections.

**One-sentence takeaway** – USC scientists have created a new way to produce endless cancer-fighting immune cells that could improve treatments for cancer and other diseases.

articles.title: Scientists discover how exercise reverses muscle aging
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden biological mechanism that helps explain how exercise can reverse some of the damage caused by muscle aging. The key is a gene called DEAF1, which becomes overactive with age and interferes with the muscles’ ability to clear damaged proteins and repair themselves. Exercise can help restore this balance, allowing older muscles to rebuild and regain strength, although the benefits may diminish when the system becomes too disrupted.
articles.content:
Scientists have uncovered a biological mechanism that helps explain how exercise protects aging muscles and restores their ability to repair themselves. The discovery reveals why physical activity can counteract some of the changes that weaken muscles with age and points toward potential new treatments for age-related muscle loss.

The research, led by Duke-NUS Medical School in collaboration with Singapore General Hospital and Cardiff University, identified a molecular system that becomes disrupted as muscles grow older. Exercise can help bring this system back into balance, allowing muscle cells to remove damaged proteins and maintain healthy tissue.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the findings provide new insight into the biology of muscle aging. They also help explain why exercise may be more effective for some older individuals than others.

Although the experiments were conducted in fruit flies and mice, the researchers believe the underlying mechanism could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to preserving muscle strength and mobility in humans.

Why Muscles Become Weaker With Age

Muscle loss is one of the most significant physical changes associated with aging. Beginning around midlife, muscles gradually lose strength and function, making everyday activities more difficult and increasing the likelihood of falls and broken bones.

Weaker muscles can also complicate recovery from injuries and illnesses and make it harder for the body to regulate blood sugar. Because muscles play an important role in metabolism, their deterioration can affect far more than physical strength.

For aging populations, including Singapore's, maintaining muscle health is especially important. Preventing muscle decline can help older adults remain independent while reducing the demands placed on caregivers and healthcare systems.

At the cellular level, keeping muscles healthy requires a careful balance between producing new proteins and disposing of old or damaged ones. Proteins form much of the machinery and structure within muscle cells, so this ongoing maintenance is essential for normal function.

One of the main systems responsible for regulating this process is a signaling pathway called mTORC1. It acts as a growth regulator, helping cells determine when to manufacture proteins and support muscle maintenance.

However, this system can become less balanced with age.

When mTORC1 becomes excessively active, muscle cells may devote too much attention to producing proteins while failing to clear away damaged ones. Over time, these defective proteins accumulate, placing stress on cells and interfering with their ability to function properly.

Scientists have long recognized this imbalance as a contributor to muscle deterioration, but the mechanism responsible for pushing the system out of balance remained unclear.

Scientists Discover a Key Gene Behind Muscle Aging

The researchers traced the problem to a gene called DEAF1, which appears to play an important role in controlling how muscles age.

As muscles grow older, DEAF1 levels can increase. The team discovered that this rise drives excessive mTORC1 activity, disrupting the normal cycle of protein production and removal.

The result is a breakdown in muscle maintenance. Instead of efficiently replacing damaged components and preserving healthy tissue, aging muscle cells become increasingly burdened by proteins that should have been cleared away.

Under normal circumstances, DEAF1 is regulated by a family of proteins known as FOXOs.

These proteins help control gene activity and are involved in important cellular maintenance processes. In healthy muscles, they prevent DEAF1 from becoming excessively active.

But FOXO activity tends to decline with age. As this protective regulation weakens, DEAF1 can increase, driving mTORC1 activity higher and further disrupting the processes needed to maintain muscle health.

The researchers found that this chain of events helps explain why aging muscles gradually lose their capacity to repair themselves.

Crucially, they also discovered that exercise can interrupt the process.

How Exercise Helps Aging Muscles Repair Themselves

Exercise does more than stimulate muscles to grow stronger. According to the findings, physical activity can also help restore the cellular maintenance system that becomes disrupted during aging.

The researchers found that exercise activates regulatory proteins that reduce DEAF1 levels. This helps return mTORC1 activity to a healthier balance, allowing muscle cells to remove damaged proteins while continuing to produce the new proteins they need.

In effect, exercise helps muscles perform an important internal cleanup, making it easier for them to maintain healthy tissue and recover from damage.

Assistant Professor Tang Hong-Wen, the study's lead author from the Cancer and Stem Cell Biology Program at Duke-NUS, explained:

"Exercise can reverse this process, correcting the imbalance. Physical activity activates certain proteins which lower DEAF1 levels, bringing the growth pathway back into balance. This allows aging muscles to clear out damaged proteins, rebuild themselves properly, and help them stay stronger and more resilient."

However, the researchers discovered an important limitation.

When DEAF1 levels become extremely elevated or FOXO activity falls too low, exercise may no longer be sufficient to fully restore normal muscle repair.

This suggests that the biological condition of muscle cells can influence how effectively they respond to physical activity. It also offers a possible explanation for why some older adults experience greater improvements from exercise than others.

The findings do not suggest that exercise loses its value with age. Rather, they indicate that understanding the biological changes occurring inside aging muscles may be necessary to develop more effective strategies for preventing muscle decline.

Experiments Reveal a Way to Restore Muscle Strength

To investigate the role of DEAF1, the researchers performed experiments using fruit flies and older mice.

These two animal models allowed the team to examine whether the same biological mechanism influences muscle health across very different species.

The results revealed a consistent pattern.

When the researchers increased DEAF1 levels, muscles weakened rapidly. But when they reduced DEAF1, the balance between protein production and removal improved, and muscle strength was restored.

Finding similar effects in both fruit flies and mice suggests that DEAF1 participates in an evolutionarily conserved system, meaning the underlying biological function has been maintained across species over long periods of evolution.

These experiments also provided evidence that DEAF1 is not simply associated with muscle deterioration. Changing its levels directly affected muscle function, strengthening the case that it plays an important role in the aging process.

Whether targeting this system can produce comparable benefits in humans remains to be established.

Could Scientists Mimic the Benefits of Exercise?

The implications of the discovery may extend beyond ordinary muscle aging.

DEAF1 also influences muscle stem cells, which are specialized cells that help repair and regenerate muscle tissue after injury or damage.

As people age, these cells become less effective, and their numbers or activity can decline, making recovery more difficult. Disruptions involving DEAF1 may further impair the body's ability to regenerate healthy muscle.

By identifying DEAF1 as an important regulator, researchers have uncovered a potential target for therapies designed to improve muscle maintenance and recovery.

Such treatments could eventually benefit people who have difficulty exercising, including those recovering from major surgery, serious illness, or chronic conditions such as cancer.

One possibility is that adjusting DEAF1 activity could reproduce some of the molecular changes normally triggered by physical activity. This might help preserve muscle strength even when a person's ability to exercise is limited.

However, this remains a potential future application rather than an established treatment. Further research will be needed to determine whether manipulating DEAF1 is both safe and effective in humans.

Priscillia Choy Sze Mun, the study's first author and a research assistant in the Cancer and Stem Cell Biology Program at Duke-NUS, described the discovery:

"Exercise tells muscles to 'clean up and reset.' Lowering DEAF1 helps older muscles regain strength and balance, almost like hitting the rewind button. With millions of older adults at risk of muscle decline, understanding DEAF1 could lead to new ways to protect muscles and improve quality of life."

A New Direction for Fighting Age-Related Muscle Loss

The findings highlight an important distinction between simply stimulating muscle growth and maintaining the cellular systems that keep muscles healthy.

Producing more proteins is not always beneficial if damaged proteins are allowed to accumulate. Effective muscle maintenance requires both processes to work together.

By showing how exercise helps restore this balance, the researchers have identified a potential biological explanation for some of its protective effects against muscle aging.

Professor Patrick Tan, Senior Vice-Dean for Research at Duke-NUS, emphasized the broader significance:

"This study helps explain, at a molecular level, why aging muscles lose their ability to repair themselves and why exercise can restore that balance in some individuals. By identifying DEAF1 as a key regulator in this process, these findings may lead to new ways in which the benefits of exercise can be brought to societies with rapidly aging populations."

The discovery may ultimately help researchers design interventions that complement physical activity, particularly for people whose muscles no longer respond as effectively to exercise.

For now, the research reinforces the importance of exercise while revealing that its benefits depend on an intricate network of molecular processes inside muscle cells.

As populations around the world grow older, understanding these processes could become increasingly valuable for protecting mobility, supporting recovery, and helping people maintain their independence later in life.

Duke-NUS Medical School combines medical education with basic and translational biomedical research. Its work aims to improve understanding of common diseases and translate laboratory discoveries into new approaches to treatment, benefiting patients in Singapore and internationally.

This work was supported by the Singapore Ministry of Education (2022-MOET1-0004, FY2025-MOET1-0004), Diana Koh Innovative Cancer Research Award (Duke-NUS-DKICRA/2024/0001), National Academy of Medicine (MOH-001189-00), and the Singapore Ministry of Health through the National Medical Research Council (NMRC) Office, MOH Holdings Pte Ltd under the NMRC (MOH-001208-00, MOH-001885-00, MOH-001831-00).

Authors Qian Gou and Priya D Gopal Krishnan received support from the Khoo Postdoctoral Fellowship (Duke-NUS-KPFA/2025/0078; Duke-NUS-KPFA/2024/0075).

articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques découvrent comment l'exercice inverse le vieillissement musculaire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En vieillissant, les muscles deviennent souvent plus faibles et ont moins de capacité à se réparer, ce qui rend les activités quotidiennes plus difficiles et augmente le risque de blessures. Les scientifiques cherchent à comprendre pourquoi les muscles vieillissent et comment l'exercice les aide à rester forts.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de la Duke-NUS Medical School, de l'hôpital général de Singapour et de l'université de Cardiff ont découvert qu'un gène appelé DEAF1 joue un rôle clé dans le vieillissement des muscles. En vieillissant, ce gène devient trop actif, ce qui perturbe la gestion des protéines endommagées dans les cellules musculaires. L'exercice réduit le niveau de DEAF1, permettant aux muscles d'éliminer les parties abîmées et de se reconstruire plus forts. L'étude a été réalisée sur des mouches des fruits et des souris et publiée dans la revue scientifique PNAS.

**Impact** – Cette découverte explique pourquoi l'exercice peut restaurer la force musculaire chez les personnes âgées en rééquilibrant un processus interne dans les cellules musculaires. Elle montre aussi pourquoi certains bénéficient plus que d'autres de l'exercice, selon l'état biologique de leurs muscles. Comprendre DEAF1 pourrait permettre de développer de nouveaux traitements pour ceux qui ne peuvent pas faire d'exercice facilement.

**Étape suivante** – Les scientifiques vont étudier si cibler DEAF1 peut améliorer la santé musculaire chez l'humain en toute sécurité. Cela pourrait conduire à des médicaments qui reproduisent les effets de l'exercice et aident à préserver la force musculaire chez les personnes peu actives. D'autres recherches testeront comment appliquer ces découvertes en traitements.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les scientifiques ont découvert que l'exercice réduit l'activité du gène DEAF1, aidant les muscles âgés à éliminer les dommages et à retrouver de la force, ce qui pourrait ouvrir la voie à de futurs traitements contre la perte musculaire.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren cómo el ejercicio revierte el envejecimiento muscular
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – A medida que las personas envejecen, sus músculos suelen debilitarse y tienen menos capacidad para repararse, lo que dificulta las actividades diarias y aumenta el riesgo de lesiones. Los científicos buscan entender por qué envejecen los músculos y cómo el ejercicio ayuda a mantenerlos fuertes.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Duke-NUS Medical School, el Hospital General de Singapur y la Universidad de Cardiff descubrieron que un gen llamado DEAF1 juega un papel clave en el envejecimiento muscular. Con la edad, este gen se vuelve demasiado activo, causando problemas en cómo las células musculares manejan las proteínas dañadas. El ejercicio ayuda a reducir los niveles de DEAF1, lo que permite que los músculos eliminen las partes dañadas y se reconstruyan más fuertes. El estudio se realizó en moscas de la fruta y ratones, y fue publicado en la revista científica PNAS.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento explica por qué el ejercicio puede restaurar la fuerza muscular en personas mayores al corregir un equilibrio interno dentro de las células musculares. También muestra por qué algunos adultos mayores se benefician más del ejercicio que otros, dependiendo del estado biológico de sus músculos. Entender DEAF1 podría conducir a nuevos tratamientos para personas que tienen dificultades para hacer ejercicio.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos planean estudiar si dirigir DEAF1 puede mejorar la salud muscular en humanos de forma segura. Esto podría llevar a medicamentos que imiten los efectos del ejercicio, ayudando a preservar la fuerza muscular en personas con poca actividad. Se necesitarán más investigaciones para aplicar estos hallazgos en tratamientos reales.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Científicos descubrieron que el ejercicio reduce la actividad del gen DEAF1, ayudando a los músculos envejecidos a eliminar daños y recuperar fuerza, lo que podría guiar futuros tratamientos contra la pérdida muscular.

articles.title: Can a positive mindset protect us from the sniffles?
articles.summary: If you’re trying to avoid the worst of cold and flu season, looking after your mind can help shape your immune system, finds columnist David Robson
articles.content:
If you’re trying to avoid the worst of cold and flu season, looking after your mind can help shape your immune system, finds columnist David Robson

Mindfulness can help your immune system fight off the sniffles Connect Images/Getty Images

The threat seems to be everywhere. On the tube, on the bus, as I the queue for coffee, I find that I am surrounded by coughs and sneezes, spreading diseases.

I eat healthily, exercise and try to get 8 hours of sleep to fend off the dreaded lurgy. It is only recently, however, that I started wondering whether our mental life might also play a part in our body’s defences. And the more I dug into the available literature, the more convinced I have become that it is critical.

Our attitudes, I have discovered, can subtly shape our immune system’s activity, which directly influences how likely we are to develop symptoms. If we want to fend off infection, we would do well to look after our minds as well as our bodies.

Advertisement

One of the first studies to explore this possibility arrived in the early 2000s, when Sheldon Cohen at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and his colleagues recruited 334 plucky volunteers who were willing to be infected with the common cold. In the month before the trial, they took regular questionnaires about their feelings throughout the day, noting emotions both positive (cheerful, at ease, energetic) and negative (sad, on edge, hostile).

On infection day, the scientists gave each participant a nasal drop containing one of two rhinoviruses known to cause sniffles, then held them in quarantine for five more days to observe whether any symptoms developed – quantified through objective measures. The team estimated the participants’ mucus production, for example, by collecting and weighing the snotty tissues they had used.

Cohen’s results were unequivocal. People with a sunnier emotional style were about a third less likely to develop symptoms than those who were less positive. Quite amazingly, the influence of the positive feelings was independent of the negative feelings – meaning that people who managed to feel both cheerful and anxious, for instance, were still less likely to develop symptoms than those who were neither cheerful nor anxious. This may sound counterintuitive, but it is perfectly possible to feel multiple emotions at the same time, and Cohen’s results seemed to suggest that positive feelings play the greatest role in our health.

I might have been sceptical if this were the only evidence, but multiple other studies have since confirmed and extended these findings. Cohen and his colleagues have shown that a so-called positive emotional style (PES) could also protect participants from influenza, for example – even after they controlled for a host of factors including age, sex, education, race and body mass.

While the exact mechanisms are unclear, it almost certainly comes down to stress, which is known to throw our defences into disarray. Someone under a lot of pressure may struggle to summon the resources to identify the virus when it first takes hold, leading to a suppressed immune response. Alternatively, the immune system may leap into action too quickly and too eagerly, bombarding the body with the inflammation that lies behind many of our symptoms.

In the case of the common cold, it seems that the second potential mechanism is the most relevant. Someone with a more positive frame of mind may find it easier to cope with life’s stresses, meaning that the body becomes less inflamed when they face a pathogen. Along these lines, Cohen has found that people’s symptoms, such as a runny nose, are directly correlated with their levels of IL-6, a pro-inflammatory signalling protein called a cytokine, after infection. This was much lower among those with a PES. A group of researchers led by Sara Puig Pérez at Valencian National University, Spain, meanwhile, found that optimists have lower levels of another pro-inflammatory cytokine, TNFα, which has been linked to the fatigue and lethargy that often accompanies our sniffles, and this seemed to be reflected in fewer overall symptoms. It seems that the optimist’s body is simply better able to fine tune its response to the threat at hand.

As fascinating as this is, I’m mostly interested in the ways that I might use this information to protect myself, so I was delighted to find a trial of an eight-week mindfulness course by Bruce Barrett at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and his colleagues. Like Cohen, Barrett looked for objective evidence of infection, with blood tests, cheek swabs and nasal washes, rather than relying solely on reported symptoms.

The mindfulness course had previously been shown to cultivate a more positive mindset – and this had the desired effect on the participants’ health. The participants were generally less likely to develop a respiratory illness after practicing mindfulness. And for those who did develop signs of an infection, the symptoms were less severe. The benefits were comparable to those of exercise, which is also known to increase the efficiency of the immune system. The meditators were also less likely to take time off work due to illness than the control group, who had been put on a waiting list for the course.

Mindfulness may not be your thing. As I’ve written previously, I’ve personally struggled with it in the past, although I’m now finding new ways to incorporate it into my life. Given the very general link to good feelings, I’m sure that plenty of other kinds of self-care would bring similar protection. Social connection also seems to boost the immune response, so you might try to reach out to the people who matter most to you, for instance.

With the nights drawing in over the northern hemisphere, it is very easy to succumb to the winter blues, so now could be the perfect time to focus on the things that bring you comfort. A sneeze-free sniffle season may just be one of many benefits.

This has broad significance for public health, offering accessible, non-pharmaceutical ways to enhance wellbeing during cold and flu seasons. The article provides detailed evidence from multiple studies, including controlled trials, making the story substantive and focused.

articles.title: WHO scales up Ebola readiness in 22 countries across three continents
articles.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) is strengthening Ebola preparedness amid conflict and displacement affecting millions of lives in a region that spans parts of Africa, Asia and Europe.
articles.content:
The UN agency’s eastern Mediterranean region comprises 22 countries and territories. Intensified support is being given to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan, which have been identified as priority countries.

This follows deadly outbreaks of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus in both the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda and confirmation of a case in Kenya linked to the DRC.

Soundcloud

Hostilities and overstretched health systems

Although there have not been any Ebola cases in the region so far, conflict, displacement and overstretched health systems in several countries are making it difficult to prepare and respond should the situation change.

In a speech earlier this week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Gebreyesus described the region as “the epicentre of global humanitarian need”.

More than 117 million people in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Sudan, Syria, Yemen and beyond, require humanitarian assistance to survive.

Assessing readiness, identifying challenges

Between July and September, WHO deployed missions to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan to assess national readiness and identify challenges in Ebola surveillance, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, case management and emergency coordination.

The UN agency is helping authorities to address gaps through training, technical support, medical supplies and simulation exercises.

It has developed regional readiness checklists, contingency planning tools and technical guidance, in addition to strengthening coordination with countries in both Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean.

WHO has also provided laboratory supplies, traveller guidance and community engagement resources.

Despite progress, gaps remain in early detection, laboratory confirmation and availability of protective equipment and resources for emergency response.

“Conflict, insecurity and restricted access present additional challenges, particularly in countries already facing major humanitarian emergencies,” WHO said.

Meanwhile, work continues to ensure that national authorities and partners can rapidly detect, investigate and manage suspected Ebola cases.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: WHO boosts Ebola preparedness across 22 countries facing health challenges
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The World Health Organization (WHO) is working to stop the spread of Ebola, a deadly virus. Recent outbreaks have happened in parts of Africa, and some cases have been linked to nearby countries. Many countries in Africa, Asia, and Europe face problems like conflict and weak health systems, making it harder to fight diseases.

**What happened** – WHO is improving Ebola readiness in 22 countries in its eastern Mediterranean region. It is focusing on Djibouti, Somalia, and Sudan by sending experts to check how ready these countries are, helping with training, providing medical supplies, and running practice drills. This work started after Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, and a case in Kenya.

**Impact** – This effort helps countries prepare better by finding and fixing problems in tracking Ebola, testing for the virus, controlling infections, and managing patients. Even though no Ebola cases have been found yet in these 22 countries, being prepared is important because many people are affected by war and displacement, which makes health care harder. The WHO’s support aims to protect millions of people by making sure health teams can quickly detect and respond to Ebola.

**What's next step** – WHO will continue working with national health teams to improve early detection and emergency response. They will provide more supplies, training, and coordination to close remaining gaps. The goal is to make sure these countries can act fast if Ebola appears, despite challenges like conflict and limited access.

**One-sentence takeaway** – WHO is helping 22 countries strengthen their ability to detect and respond to Ebola, reducing risks for millions living in difficult conditions.
